explanations.answer: They're filled with awe and run to greet Him
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what the text says: "As soon as all the people saw Jesus, they were filled with awe and ran to greet Him." (Mark 9:15) Picture it, baker. A crowd mid-argument, and the second He shows up, they take off running toward Him. Nobody finished their sentence. I think the awe hit before the arguing even had time to stop.

explanations.answer: They go quiet and slowly back away from Him
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody is backing up here. The text says the people "were filled with awe and ran to greet Him." (Mark 9:15) They went toward Jesus, and fast. Slowly tiptoeing away is what I did when the drawer opened and I thought it was cleaning day.

explanations.answer: They keep on arguing and pay Him no mind
explanations.explanation: The argument didn't survive His arrival. Mark 9:15 says that as soon as all the people saw Jesus, they were filled with awe and ran to greet Him. Nobody ignored Him, friend. The scribes were arguing right up until that moment, and then the whole crowd had somewhere better to run.

Right, baker. The dad says, "I asked Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable." (Mark 9:18) He doesn't say they refused or ran off. He says they couldn't do it. Later in the house, the disciples ask Jesus why, so they were wondering the same thing (Mark 9:28).

Close, but that's not the word. The dad says the disciples "were unable." (Mark 9:18) That's different from not wanting to. They were asked to drive it out, and it didn't happen. Later they come to Jesus privately and ask, "Why couldn't we drive it out?" (Mark 9:28), and that sounds like men who wanted to.

The text never says the disciples were afraid. The dad says they "were unable." (Mark 9:18) That's all he tells us. I'd be careful about adding feelings the verse doesn't give us. The word is unable, and that's the one that fits.

Yes! Jesus says, "Bring the boy to Me." (Mark 9:19) Notice what He does after that whole sigh about the generation. He doesn't walk off. He asks for the boy. I think that's the best part of the verse, because the next thing He wants is the one who needs help.
That's the opposite of what happens. Jesus says, "Bring the boy to Me." (Mark 9:19) He wants the boy brought closer, not sent away. Nobody in this crowd is going home until this boy has met Jesus.

Jesus doesn't send them off to try again on their own. He says, "Bring the boy to Me." (Mark 9:19) He steps in Himself. Trying again alone is how I handled a jammed cookie box lid for a whole week, and I do not recommend it.

True. Mark 9:20 says, "So they brought him, and seeing Jesus, the spirit immediately threw the boy into a convulsion." The boy fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. It's a hard moment to read, and I think this one hurts. Jesus is right there, though.

It's actually true. The text says, "So they brought him, and seeing Jesus, the spirit immediately threw the boy into a convulsion." (Mark 9:20) The boy fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. I think this is a heavy part of the story. Jesus is already there with him.
This one is false, baker. Jesus asks, "How long has this been with him?" and the father answers, "From childhood." (Mark 9:21) That's not recent at all. It's been a very long road for that family.

Right, it's false. When Jesus asks how long this has been with the boy, the father says, "From childhood." (Mark 9:21) Nothing recent about it. A dad who has carried this since his son was small is a dad who knows how heavy it gets.

That's the one. The dad says, "But if You can do anything…" and Jesus answers, "If You can?" (Mark 9:22-23) He picks up those words and hands them right back. Then He says, "All things are possible to him who believes!" (Mark 9:23). The echo makes the dad stop and hear himself.

Not quite. The dad does ask Jesus to "help us," but that's not the part Jesus echoes. Jesus says, "If You can?" (Mark 9:23), repeating the dad's "if You can do anything" from verse 22. The help is the part Jesus goes on to give.

The dad does ask Jesus to "have compassion on us" (Mark 9:22), but that's not what Jesus echoes. He repeats the "if You can" part and says, "If You can?" (Mark 9:23). Nothing in the text says He is brushing off the compassion request. The echo goes to the "if."

explanations.answer: He believes and asks for help with his unbelief
explanations.explanation: That's it, and I love how honest it is. The father cries out, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24) He doesn't dress it up. He says both parts out loud and asks Jesus for help with the second one. I think that's about as real a prayer as a person can pray.

explanations.answer: He has always believed without a single doubt
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that, friend. He cries out, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24) A man with no doubt wouldn't ask for help with unbelief. He's honest about where he is, and he brings it right to Jesus.

explanations.answer: He doesn't believe at all and needs a sign
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says. The father cries out, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24) He starts with "I do believe." Then he asks for help with the part that's still shaky. He never asks for a sign.

This is false, baker. Jesus says, "I command you to come out and never enter him again." (Mark 9:25) Never. He doesn't leave the door open for a return trip. The command goes out and it covers the boy for good.
Correct, it's false. Jesus tells the spirit, "I command you to come out and never enter him again." (Mark 9:25) There's no "maybe later" in that sentence. He closes the door behind it.

True. After the boy became like a corpse, Mark 9:27 says, "But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up." Look at that sequence, baker. Many were saying he was dead, and then Jesus' hand, and then the boy standing. I think that's the moment the whole crowd stops talking.

It's actually true. The text says, "But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up." (Mark 9:27) This comes right after many said, "He is dead." (Mark 9:26) Jesus reaches down, takes his hand, and the boy stands.

That's the answer. Jesus says, "This kind cannot come out, except by prayer." (Mark 9:29) The disciples asked Him privately, and He gave them a straight answer. Short, simple, and worth keeping in the oven of your heart.

Practice is a good word for baking, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says, "This kind cannot come out, except by prayer." (Mark 9:29) I stamped cookies for years and still blurred my lines, so practice only gets you so far. The word here is prayer.

Patience is a good thing to have, baker, but that's not the word. Jesus says, "This kind cannot come out, except by prayer." (Mark 9:29) The disciples asked Him why they couldn't do it, and prayer is what He named.
